facts.statehood_note: Texas was an independent nation, the Republic of Texas, from 1836 until it joined the United States. Texas voters approved annexation on October 13, 1845, and President James K. Polk signed the resolution admitting Texas as the 28th state on December 29, 1845.

symbols.name: Bluebonnet (1901, the first Texas state symbol)

facts.name_origin: "Tejas" is the Spanish spelling of "taysha," a Caddo word that means "friend" or "ally." Indigenous peoples in the area used the word widely before the Spanish arrived. This is why the state motto is "Friendship."

government.chambers: Texas Senate (31 members, one for each of 31 districts) and Texas House of Representatives (150 members, each elected for a two-year term). The Legislature meets for no more than 140 days, starting in January of odd-numbered years.
government.executive: Governor, the head of the executive branch, elected to a 4-year term with no term limit (a 1972 amendment changed the term from two years to four). The Governor can call the Legislature back for special meetings of up to 30 days.
government.courts: Texas has two highest courts: the Supreme Court of Texas (one chief justice and eight justices) has the final say in civil cases, and the Court of Criminal Appeals (one presiding judge and eight judges) has the final say in criminal cases. Below them are courts of appeals, district courts, county courts, justice of the peace courts, and city (municipal) courts.
government.local: 254 counties, more than any other state. Each county is run by a Commissioners' Court that includes four elected commissioners. Cities and school districts have their own local governments. Texas also has three federally recognized tribal nations with their own governments.
government.constitution: Texas has had several constitutions (1845, 1861, 1866, 1869). The current Texas Constitution was written at a convention in 1875 and adopted by voters on February 15, 1876. Article 1 is the Bill of Rights.
government.kid_line: "Equality under the law shall not be denied or abridged because of sex, race, color, creed, or national origin." (Texas Constitution, Article 1, Section 3a)

long_ago.about: The Caddo lived in eastern and northeastern Texas and nearby Louisiana, Arkansas, and Oklahoma. They farmed corn, beans, and squash, lived in permanent villages of tall grass houses (40 to 50 feet high), made engraved pottery, and their ancestors built large earth mounds.
Jumano people lived in the Trans-Pecos region of West Texas. Some moved from place to place hunting bison, while others farmed along the Rio Grande and Concho River.
The Comanche rode horses and hunted bison across northwestern Texas and nearby lands, which the Spanish called Comanchería. They lived in tipis and became expert riders and traders.
Apache peoples used tipis and carried loads with tump lines. The Mescalero Apache roasted mescal (agave) in earth ovens.
Wichita women grew squash, pumpkins, and gourds, and saved dried squash for winter by braiding it into mats.
The Tonkawa lived in villages in central Texas and, like other Plains peoples, used tipis.

today.about: Has a reservation in Polk County in East Texas; the Alabama received a land grant there in 1854, and some Coushatta settled there in 1859.
Owns land bought in 1983 in southern Maverick County near El Indio, close to the Rio Grande.
The Tigua people live on tribal land near El Paso; their ancestors were forced into Texas from New Mexico by the Spanish after the Pueblo Revolt of 1680.

first_peoples.today_note: Texas has three federally recognized tribes with reservations in the state. By the 1890s, the U.S. government had forced most other Indigenous peoples of Texas onto reservations in present-day Oklahoma. Many Caddo were moved to Indian Territory in 1859 (the Caddo Nation is now headquartered in Binger, Oklahoma), and the Comanche were placed on the Fort Sill reservation (the Comanche Nation is now headquartered in Lawton, Oklahoma).
sites: Ysleta del Sur Pueblo, El Paso (home of the Tigua people)
Mission San Antonio de Valero (the Alamo), San Antonio, founded in 1718; the first people at the mission were Payaya, Jarame, and Pamaya Indigenous peoples
Palo Duro Canyon (site of the Battle of Palo Duro Canyon, the end of the Red River War)

history.event: Ancestors of the Caddo are part of the Caddoan Mississippian culture, farming and building large earth mounds in the region that includes northeast Texas.
Estevanico, an African man, arrives in Texas with the Spanish explorer Álvar Núñez Cabeza de Vaca. He is the first known Black person in Texas.
After the Pueblo Revolt in New Mexico, the Spanish force Tigua people south into Texas, near present-day El Paso.
Spanish Franciscans found Mission San Antonio de Valero (later called the Alamo) in San Antonio. Payaya, Jarame, and Pamaya peoples are among the first to live at the mission.

Texans of Mexican and American heritage rebel against Mexico's government. Delegates declare independence on March 2. Mexican troops besiege the Alamo for 13 days, and Tejanos (Texans of Mexican descent) are among the defenders who die. Texas wins at San Jacinto on April 21 and becomes the Republic of Texas.
The Republic of Texas constitution protects slavery. About 5,000 of the roughly 38,470 people in Texas are enslaved.
A Republic of Texas law bans free Black people from moving in and orders free Black people to leave.
Texas joins the United States as the 28th state, as a state that allows slavery.
Texas grants the Alabama people land in Polk County (1854). In 1859, many Caddo people are forced out of Texas to Indian Territory (present-day Oklahoma).
About 182,000 African Americans are enslaved in Texas, about 30 percent of all the people in the state.

A state convention votes to leave the Union on February 1, and voters approve it on February 23. Texas joins the Confederacy in March. Former President of the Republic Sam Houston protests joining the Confederacy.

U.S. Army troops arrive in Galveston, and Major General Gordon Granger reads General Order No. 3: "all slaves are free." About 250,000 Black Texans learn of their freedom. Freed people celebrate the day as Juneteenth starting in 1866.

During Reconstruction, Black Texans serve in the state legislature and constitutional conventions (52 African American men served in these roles in the late 1800s). Texas is readmitted to the Union on March 30, 1870.

In the Red River War, the U.S. Army forces the last free Comanche bands onto a reservation; Quanah Parker's band surrenders in 1875. Texas voters adopt the current state constitution on February 15, 1876.

trailblazers.name: Matthew Gaines
trailblazers.text: Matthew Gaines was born enslaved in Louisiana and later held in Texas. He became one of the first two African Americans elected to the Texas Senate, serving from 1870 to 1874, and in 1875 he was arrested in Giddings, Texas, for giving a civil rights speech.

trailblazers.name: Quanah Parker
trailblazers.text: Quanah Parker was a Quahadi Comanche chief who led the last free Comanche band until it surrendered in 1875 and moved to the Fort Sill reservation. He later worked to get better deals for his people, became a rancher, and helped found the Native American Church.

trailblazers.name: Henry Ossian Flipper
trailblazers.group: Black American man, soldier and engineer
trailblazers.text: In 1877, Henry O. Flipper became the first African American to graduate from West Point. He served with the 10th Cavalry at Texas forts including Fort Concho and Fort Davis, and later worked as an engineer and surveyor in Texas and Mexico.

trailblazers.name: Jovita Idar
trailblazers.group: Mexican American woman, teacher and journalist
trailblazers.text: Jovita Idar was a teacher, journalist, and activist who wrote for her family's newspaper, La Crónica. In 1911 she helped organize El Primer Congreso Mexicanista, a gathering of Mexican Americans, and she once stood in a newspaper's doorway to block Texas Rangers sent to shut it down.

trailblazers.name: Bessie Coleman
trailblazers.group: Black and Native American woman, aviator
trailblazers.text: Bessie Coleman grew up in Waxahachie, Texas, where she worked in cotton fields and as a laundress. American flight schools would not let her in, so she trained in France and earned an international pilot's license in 1921, becoming the first African American woman pilot (she also had Native American heritage). She later flew shows in Texas, including a Juneteenth flight in Houston.

trailblazers.name: Emma Tenayuca
trailblazers.text: Emma Tenayuca was a labor organizer and civil rights activist who led workers' strikes in the 1930s. At age 21 she led the Pecan Shellers' Strike in San Antonio, which grew to about 12,000 workers and lasted three months. In 1991 she was named to the San Antonio Women's Hall of Fame.

trailblazers.name: Selena Quintanilla
trailblazers.text: Selena, born in Lake Jackson and raised in Corpus Christi, was called "the Queen of Tejano." In 1994 she became the first female Tejano singer to win a Grammy for Best Mexican-American Album, and in 1995 she became the first Latina artist whose album reached No. 1 on the Billboard 200.

landforms: Guadalupe Peak, the highest point in Texas (about 8,750 feet), in the Trans-Pecos mountains
Palo Duro Canyon, carved by water and wind
The Caprock Escarpment, a long cliff edge between the High Plains and the Rolling Plains
Enchanted Rock, a giant granite dome in the Llano Uplift near Fredericksburg
Barrier islands along the Gulf Coast, such as Padre Island
waters: Rio Grande (the largest river; it forms the border with Mexico)
Caddo Lake, the only natural lake in Texas
Edwards Aquifer, a huge underground water supply under the Edwards Plateau
geography.regions: Texas has 10 ecoregions: the Piney Woods, Gulf Prairies and Marshes, Post Oak Savannah, Blackland Prairies, Cross Timbers, South Texas Plains, Edwards Plateau, Rolling Plains, High Plains, and Trans-Pecos.

ecosystems.name: Piney Woods
ecosystems.about: Rolling hills in East Texas covered with pines, oaks, and tall hardwood trees. National forests and the Big Thicket Nature Preserve protect its plants and animals.

ecosystems.name: Gulf Coast Prairies and Marshes
ecosystems.about: Barrier islands, salt grass marshes, and river bottomlands from Orange to South Padre Island. Padre Island wildflowers include Rio Grande phlox, Texas prickly pear, and sea lavender, and nine national wildlife refuges protect coastal wildlife.

ecosystems.name: Edwards Plateau (Hill Country)
ecosystems.about: A land of springs, stony hills, and steep canyons, with limestone full of caves. The Edwards Aquifer, a huge underground water supply, lies beneath its eastern part.

ecosystems.name: Trans-Pecos
ecosystems.about: West Texas desert valleys with creosote bush and mountain slopes with piñon pine, junipers, and oaks. In Big Bend, bluebonnets can grow two to three feet tall.

science.weather: Texas gets hurricanes from the Gulf of Mexico: the 1900 Galveston hurricane was the deadliest natural disaster in U.S. history, and Hurricane Harvey (2017) caused huge floods around Houston. Texas averages about 139 tornadoes a year, the High Plains have had long droughts, and Winter Storm Uri (2021) caused a major power crisis.
science.resources: Texas has major energy, agriculture, technology, manufacturing, and aerospace industries. Oil became important after the Spindletop oil discovery in 1901, and cattle ranching and cotton have long been big parts of the economy.
science.highlight: Endangered species comeback: Whooping cranes are an endangered bird found in Texas. Protection helped their numbers grow from only 18 birds. Most endangered plants and animals of Texas are threatened by loss of habitat.

g3_ss.title: Texas's Communities and Government
g3_ss.plan: Locate Austin and Houston on a map, learn the 254 counties idea, and compare the jobs of the Texas Legislature (31 senators, 150 representatives), the Governor, and the two highest courts; read Article 1, Section 3a of the Texas Constitution together.

g3_ss.title: Texas's First Peoples
g3_ss.plan: Compare how the Caddo (farmers in grass houses), Jumano, Comanche, and Wichita lived, then meet the three nations in Texas today: the Alabama-Coushatta Tribe of Texas, the Kickapoo Traditional Tribe of Texas, and Ysleta del Sur Pueblo; learn that "Texas" comes from the Caddo word for friend.

g3_ss.title: Texas Trailblazers
g3_ss.plan: Make trading cards for Bessie Coleman, Jovita Idar, Emma Tenayuca, Henry O. Flipper, and Selena, telling what barrier each person broke.

g45_ss.title: Texas's First Nations
g45_ss.plan: Map Caddo, Jumano, Comanche, Apache, Wichita, and Tonkawa homelands; trace the Caddo mound-building past; discuss the 1859 Caddo removal and how most nations were forced to Oklahoma by the 1890s, and who lives in Texas today.

g45_ss.title: Spanish and Mexican Texas, 1528–1836
g45_ss.plan: Follow Estevanico and Cabeza de Vaca (1528), the Tigua move after 1680, and the missions of San Antonio (1718); study the Texas Revolution, including the Tejano defenders of the Alamo, and how the new Republic protected slavery.

g45_ss.title: Texas 1845–1877: Statehood, War, and Juneteenth
g45_ss.plan: Use a timeline from statehood (December 29, 1845) to secession (1861), General Order No. 3 and Juneteenth (June 19, 1865), Black legislators like Matthew Gaines, the Red River War, and the 1876 constitution.

g3_sci.title: Texas Habitats
g3_sci.plan: Sort plants and animals into Piney Woods, Gulf Coast marsh, Hill Country, and desert habitats; build a mini diorama of one.

g3_sci.title: Storms on the Gulf
g3_sci.plan: Learn how hurricanes form over warm Gulf water, read about the 1900 Galveston hurricane, and make a family storm-safety kit list.

g3_sci.title: The Whooping Crane Comeback
g3_sci.plan: Measure out a whooping crane's height, and learn how people helped the flock grow from only 18 birds.

g45_sci.title: Ten Ecoregions of Texas
g45_sci.plan: Map the 10 ecoregions and compare plants, landforms, and rainfall from the wet Piney Woods to the dry Trans-Pecos.

g45_sci.title: Water Under the Hill Country
g45_sci.plan: Model how rain soaks through limestone into the Edwards Aquifer, and discuss why protecting it matters for people and wildlife.

g45_sci.title: Wild Weather: Hurricanes, Tornadoes, and Drought
g45_sci.plan: Graph Texas tornado counts, compare hurricane floods (Harvey, 2017) with High Plains droughts, and design a weather-safety poster.
